newsitem.title: CHINA: China prepares simple farewell for Deng.
newsitem.headline: China prepares simple farewell for Deng.

text.p: China on Sunday prepared to say a simple farewell to paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, with workers at a Beijing crematorium cleaning up a funeral parlour usually used for less illustrious mortal remains.

The low-key preparations under way at western Beijing's Babaoshan crematorium were in line with Deng's wishes, but came as a disappointment to some Chinese hoping for a grander goodbye to a leader whose rule transformed their lives.

Workmen tacked black, yellow and sky blue cloth over the bare brickwork of Babaoshan's Number Two "Farewell Hall" and mopped the tiled floor as an honour guard of soldier coffin-bearers strutted through their paces nearby.
The parlour, normally available for use by ordinary Beijing residents, will house Deng's remains before the political patriarch's cremation on Monday, staff said.
A memorial service, attended by 10,000 people but with no foreign dignitaries invited, is to be held in Beijing's Great Hall of the People on Tuesday. Deng's ashes will be scattered at sea.

Deng, an early opponent of the leadership cult around his predecesser Chairman Mao Zedong, made clear that, when he died, he wanted more restrained mourning than the near-hysteria that followed Mao's death in 1976.

"I hope you will see to it that both my retirement and my funeral are simple," Deng told members of the Communist Party's Central Committee in 1989, a desire that his hand-picked heir President Jiang Zemin appears determined to fulfill.

State media have publicised a request by Deng's family that his body not be put on public display, that his corneas be donated to an eye bank and that parts of his body be offered for medical dissection.

The no-frills farewell to the nation's greatest communist reformer has come as a shock to some of the many whose lives were transformed by his 1978 rejection of ultra-left policies that had led China down an economic blind alley.
"I came all the way from Changchun (in northeast China) to see him," said farmer Hao Xingchang, who wept when he heard that Deng was to be cremated and that his body would not go on view.
"Under the policies before Deng Xiaoping we farmers were hungry. Only under Deng Xiaoping's policies could we eat our fill," he said.
Workers at Babaoshan rushed to finish Sunday morning's cremations before police sealed off the area to allow further preparations for Deng's farewell.
A shopkeeper selling paper wreaths to mourners outside Babaoshan said the closure of the crematorium would harm sales, but added he had no complaints.
"Business is bad... but you can't think about money when it comes to the funeral of a national leader," he said.
